## AINews

**Priority: HIGH**

### Top Updates
* Anthropic launched **Claude Tag**, a new **multiplayer, proactive, and persistent AI agent** that integrates with Slack, allowing teams to work with Claude as a shared team member rather than a one-to-one chatbot.
* Claude Tag enables teams to @-mention Claude in channels or threads, grant it scoped access to specific channels, tools, data, and codebases, and let it follow ongoing conversations to summarize discussions, break down tasks, and surface relevant updates over time.
* The system is designed with enterprise controls, allowing admins to tightly configure what Claude can see and do in each channel, and is currently in **beta/research preview** for Claude Enterprise and Claude Team customers on Slack.
* Anthropic's own use of similar agents, such as writing a majority of some product teams' code, is cited as a proof point for productivity impact.
* Industry commentators see Claude Tag as part of a broader competitive push among leading AI labs to own the **"operational layer"** between foundation models and day-to-day enterprise work.
* Slack is evolving into an AI-native workspace, embedding generative AI and agentic capabilities directly into chats, channels, and workflows, with features like **Slack AI**, **Slackbot**, and **Slack GPT**.
* Slack is opening its platform so AI agents and apps can safely use Slack's conversational data as context, via a new **real-time search (RTS) API**, a dedicated **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** server, and related tools.

### Notable Links
* [Claude Tag](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=1084089&post_id=203334305&isFreemail=true&r=49by34&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoyNTc1Mzg2NDAsInBvc3RfaWQiOjIwMzMzNDMwNSwiaWF0IjoxNzgyMjg1Mzc0LCJleHAiOjE3ODQ4NzczNzQsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0xMDg0MDg5Iiwic3ViIjoicG9zdC1yZWFjdGlvbiJ9.bvWJoH0iJgtiJmJkKdB4Qr2JR_nyKyoC41qbgwrnUWs)

additionalContext.topic: Advanced AI as a cyberattack vector
additionalContext.context:
In current AI/ML discussions, **advanced generative and autonomous AI systems** are increasingly viewed as potential tools and enablers for large-scale cyberattacks. Intelligence and cybersecurity agencies warn that rapidly improving foundation models—especially those capable of writing code, crafting persuasive text, and autonomously interacting with systems—could be used to automate vulnerability discovery, generate highly tailored phishing campaigns, and assist less-skilled attackers in building malware or exploiting complex software flaws.[8] This shifts AI from being primarily a defensive aid (for detection and monitoring) to also being a force multiplier for offensive cyber operations.

Recent reports highlight that national security agencies consider **AI-enabled cyber threats** to be only months to a few years away from material impact, as general-purpose models are fine‑tuned or combined with tools such as code repositories, exploit databases, and autonomous agents.[8] Industry and government responses include new AI safety evaluations focused on cyber capabilities, red‑team exercises to test how easily models can be misused, and calls for regulation or voluntary commitments to restrict high‑risk functionality. For enterprises, this means security strategies must now assume attackers may leverage AI for faster, more adaptive, and more convincing attacks, driving investment in AI‑augmented defense tools, workforce upskilling in AI-aware security practices, and tighter governance over internal use of powerful models.

More broadly, the industry impact is two‑sided: security vendors are racing to integrate **AI for threat detection and response**, while simultaneously hardening their own models against being weaponized. This is influencing procurement (e.g., requiring providers to document red‑teaming against cyber misuse), compliance (mapping AI use to emerging standards and regulations), and risk management (treating advanced AI access similarly to powerful cyber tools). As AI capability and accessibility continue to accelerate, organizations are being advised to explicitly include "AI-as-a-threat-actor" scenarios in their threat models, incident response plans, and board‑level risk discussions, recognizing AI not just as an IT feature but as a potential adversarial capability in its own right.[8]

Claude Tag is Anthropic’s new **multiplayer, proactive, and persistent AI agent** that lives inside Slack as a shared team member rather than a one‑to‑one chatbot.[3][8] Teams can @‑mention Claude in channels or threads, grant it scoped access to specific channels, tools, data, and codebases, and let it follow ongoing conversations so it can summarize discussions, break down tasks, and surface relevant updates over time without needing explicit prompts each time.[3][7][8] The system is designed with enterprise controls: admins can tightly configure what Claude can see and do in each channel, and the feature is currently in **beta/research preview** for Claude Enterprise and Claude Team customers on Slack.[7][8]

This matters because it shifts AI in the workplace from single‑user chat windows to **embedded, team‑wide agents** that participate asynchronously in real workflows, closer to how a human teammate operates.[3][6] Anthropic and external coverage frame Claude Tag as a concrete step toward always‑on, organizational agents that maintain memory across channels, orchestrate workflows, and handle background execution, permissions, and monitoring—an evolution beyond simple chat integrations.[3][6][7] Early reports highlight Anthropic’s own use of similar agents (e.g., writing a majority of some product teams’ code) as a proof point for productivity impact, and industry commentators see Claude Tag as part of a broader competitive push among leading AI labs to own the “operational layer” between foundation models and day‑to‑day enterprise work.[6][7]

Slack is a leading enterprise collaboration platform that is rapidly evolving into an AI-native workspace, embedding generative AI and agentic capabilities directly into chats, channels, and workflows. Recent releases include **Slack AI** (native summarization and Q&A over messages), a revamped **Slackbot** with generative AI for search and content creation, and **Slack GPT**/native AI that tie Slack into Salesforce’s Einstein GPT and other large language models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI models.[1][4][9][12] These features provide search answers grounded in a user’s Slack and connected data, channel and thread summaries, workflow-aware assistance, and the ability to draft or refine content within Slack itself.[1][4][9]

On the developer side, Slack is opening its platform so AI agents and apps can safely use Slack’s conversational data as context, via a new **real-time search (RTS) API**, a dedicated **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** server, and related tools.[3][8][10] This makes it possible for third-party and in‑house agents—such as Anthropic’s Claude—to search across channels, threads, and files, then respond with grounded, work-specific answers and automate tasks inside Slack.[3][8] Strategically, this positions Slack as a central AI orchestration layer for enterprise work: a secure, context-rich front end where employees interact with multiple LLMs, automate business workflows, and tap into Salesforce and other systems, with the aim of boosting productivity, decision-making, and collaboration at scale.[4][7][12]

additionalContext.topic: Zohran Mamdani (and ‘Mamdani’ as shorthand for an AI-regulating political agenda)
additionalContext.context:
In current AI/ML discourse, **“Mamdani” most often refers to Zohran Mamdani**, a New York social‑democratic politician whose recent New York City mayoral victory has been framed as a key test of how aggressively cities can regulate and re-shape the AI industry.[15] Coverage describes his administration as closely aligned with progressive tech‑skeptical allies in city and state politics, positioning him as a counterweight to both Big Tech lobbying and laissez‑faire AI policy at the national level.[14][15] Rather than being an AI model or company, “Mamdani” here functions as political shorthand for a platform that treats AI as infrastructure to be governed in the public interest rather than left to corporate self‑regulation.[14][15]

Mamdani has quickly become relevant to AI/ML practitioners because his agenda targets **AI governance, platform power, and labor impacts**. Reports note that his allies helped defeat a proposed federal amendment that would have effectively frozen AI regulation for a decade, signaling an assertive stance on algorithmic accountability and data rights.[15] In New York specifically, Mamdani has pushed for stricter rules on AI used in public services and education, including work with the city’s public school system on AI guidelines and guardrails.[11] His administration has also criticized error‑prone city AI tools—such as chatbots giving unlawful advice to businesses—as evidence that public-sector AI must be audited, transparent, and accountable.[7][8] For the AI/ML industry, the “Mamdani” moment signals a shift toward more adversarial scrutiny of foundation models, recommender systems, and AI‑driven political advertising, with New York emerging as a proving ground for how urban governments can constrain or reshape AI deployment at scale.[4][6][15]

International spy agencies in the AI/ML space are intelligence services using machine learning and generative AI to process vast data streams, support analysts, and improve cyber defense and offensive counterintelligence. Recent reporting says U.S. and U.K. agencies have publicly described using generative AI for tasks like summarization, ideation, triage, and red-teaming their own operations, while governments are also investing heavily in the compute and infrastructure needed to run frontier models.[6][5] This matters because intelligence agencies handle sensitive data and national-security operations, so AI can significantly increase speed and scale but also raises risks around secrecy, model tampering, and dependency on foreign or commercial platforms.[8][11][12]

missingStories.headline: OpenAI Quietly Restores and Expands GPT‑4o After Safety Pause
missingStories.summary: OpenAI has restored full access to its GPT‑4o model after a period of partial rollback and safety adjustments, while also pushing reliability and multimodal quality improvements for developers.[1] The update includes broader availability in the API and more stable behavior in complex reasoning and tool-use scenarios.[1] OpenAI framed the changes as part of an ongoing effort to harden its flagship model after earlier outages and safety concerns.
missingStories.whyItMatters: Many production systems had constrained or downgraded GPT‑4o usage during the pause; its restoration with improved stability lets teams safely re-enable higher-capability endpoints. For practitioners, the changes affect prompt design, reliability expectations, and how aggressively they can lean on 4o for multimodal workflows and tools.

missingStories.headline: Alibaba Announces New Qwen3 Model Family as It Ramps Global AI Push
missingStories.summary: Alibaba has introduced its **Qwen3** model line, expanding the Qwen series with new versions that target both general-purpose and coding workloads.[1] The release is part of Alibaba’s broader effort to compete globally in foundation models, offering stronger multilingual support and improved reasoning compared with earlier Qwen generations.[1]
missingStories.whyItMatters: Qwen3 gives practitioners—especially those working in or with Asian markets—more competitive options for multilingual and regionally adapted systems. The growing strength of Chinese foundation models impacts vendor selection, model evaluation, and the feasibility of building globally deployed applications without relying solely on US providers.
missingStories.source: AI News: 24 Stories You Missed While Living Your Life (segment on Alibaba announcing Qwen3 models)[1]
